newsitem.title: USA: House passes budget pact, turns back changes.
newsitem.headline: House passes budget pact, turns back changes.

text.p: The House early on Wednesday approved a five-year balanced budget agreement after narrowly defeating a key amendment that the White House warned would undermine the deal.

The House approved the budget 333-99 immediately after a cliffhanger vote of 216-214 defeated a deal-breaker amendment proposed by Transportation Committee chairman Bud Shuster. It sought to boost funds for roads and mass transit by $12 billion through the year 2002.
Anxious Republican leaders had feared until the last moment that the transportation amendment could pass and throw their budget strategy into disarray.

During the key vote House Speaker Newt Gingrich stood at the rear of the packed chamber, his white-haired head bowed as he leaned against a back railing. Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, the party's pointman in the long negotiations, made a final bid for the deal after 2 a.m. EDT (0600 GMT).

"Let's send a clear signal we are able to advance the cause of the country. Please reject the amendment. Support the agreement," Kasich, an Ohio Republican, said with a touch of resignation in his voice. He watched grim-faced as the vote teetered between victory and defeat.
On final passage, a majority of President Bill Clinton's Democrats supported the budget despite the decision by Minority Leader Richard Gephardt to oppose it.

The budget serves as the blueprint for $1.5 trillion in government spending in the coming 1998 fiscal year and sets goals for deficit reduction through 2002. The Senate also opened debate on Tuesday and was expected to pass it Thursday.

House Republican leaders had summoned rank-and-file party lawmakers to a late-night meeting on Tuesday in an attempt to salvage the budget accord. White House budget director Franklin Raines had warned in a letter that the administration strongly opposed the transportation amendment and would consider its passage a breach of the budget agreement.

But members found transporation funds, once the bread and butter of Washington politics, had become a very vexing issue. On one side they faced demands of the president and Republican leadership to stick with the budget deal and on the other side they faced demands of governors and local officials desperately seeking construction money.

All governors except Ohio's George Voinovich, a Republican, wrote to congressional leaders urging approval of the transporation funds. The budget provides $124 billion for highways and mass transit, including Amtrak passenger train line, through 2002. The increase they have sought would equal the amount paid each year by motorists in federal fuel taxes.

Shuster, R-Pa., argued that lawmakers in the full House should have the right to modify the budget agreement that was reached over four months in mainly closed-door sessions. "If we don't, we simply aren't going to have funds necessary to rebuild America as we move into the 21st century," he said.

The House also defeated amendments offered by the Congressional Black Caucus to cut defence spending by $190 billion over five years, a conservative Republican amendment to save more from domestic programmes and two other amendments that sought to increase social spending.

Gephardt, D-Mo., broke with the White House in an anticipated decision to oppose the budget. He said in a speech on the House floor he could not vote for a budget that shrank Medicare for the elderly while providing tax cuts for the wealthy.
"I refuse to be a party to an agreement that balances the budget in name only," he said. "I don't believe this budget is fair. I don't believe it invests properly in the future of our country."
Ultimtately, Democrats voted for the budget by a margin of 132-72 and Republicans voted for it by 201-26. The lone Independent, Representative Bernard Sanders of Vermont, voted no.
The budget slows the growth of government spending for the next five years, cuts Medicare by $115 billion and brings the deficit down to zero by 2002 from this year's forecast level of $67 billion.

It also provides a net $85 billion tax cut. Raines said Republican leaders had given assurances that the cut would largely benefit families with children and those in which students are seeking post-secondary education.

Congressional budget committees said that over its five years, the plan cut $304 billion in spending from what would have occurred without changes in policy but gave Clinton $33 billion to spend on education, the environment and other domestic priorities.
